transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-07-28
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 55 minutes
Recorded by: Fireflies.ai
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Samir Patel (PolarVector), Lena Novak (PolarVector), Tom Becker (PolarVector)

Summary: Introductory channel/partnership discovery. PV is a regional cloud & managed services provider focused on edge GPU racks for telco/finance customers; they're exploring bundling Redwood inference as a managed option inside their channel marketplace. Key topics: network/topology for Private (VPC) deployments, SLA and pricing expectations for a co-bundled Dedicated offering, security/compliance requirements (SOC two, SSO/SAML, KMS), and POC scoping requirements. Next: share deck + architecture docs, schedule POC scoping deep-dive.

Topics discussed:
- PV go-to-market and channel model
- Technical constraints: peering, NAT, egress, firewall, PCI/regulatory
- Deployment options: hosted API vs Dedicated vs Private/VPC/on-prem
- Performance targets: 99th perc latency, batch sizes, KV cache patterns
- Security: SOC 2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
- Commercial: pilot budget, margins, referral fees

Action items (captured): see metadata.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on partnerships. Diego (SE) and I are on to learn about PolarVector and see where we can partner, so over to you Samir for a quick intro.
[00:12] Samir Patel: Yeah thanks Maya. I'm Samir, Head of Partnerships at PolarVector, we run channel and MSP programs. Uh, we operate in EMEA and APAC, we run small clusters for telecomm and some finance clients, mostly NVIDIA-grade boxes on-prem and in colo, and we're starting to package inference stacks for customers.
[00:30] Tom Becker: Tom here in biz dev — we're looking at how to add a managed LLM inference offering without building all the runtime ourselves. So we want to understand Redwood's channel model, and technical requirements.
[00:40] Diego Alvarez: Cool, thanks. Quick one — are you thinking of reselling a hosted product, or hosting Redwood runtime in your colo as a managed private deployment?
[00:49] Lena Novak: Our preference is hybrid. For smaller customers we'd resell a hosted API with margins; for larger telco customers they'd want data residency and isolated VPC/on-prem options. So both.
[01:03] Maya Chen: That aligns with how lots of our partners start. A couple clarifying questions: typical throughput per customer, expected latency SLOs, and do you have strict key management requirements?
[01:15] Samir Patel: Throughput varies — some telco real-time NLU workloads want sub 200ms 99th perc for short prompts, others are batch scoring for embeddings. On KMS, yes some customers require customer-managed keys and no plaintext tokens stored offsite.
[01:31] Diego Alvarez: Noted. Our Private and Dedicated modes both support customer-managed KMS integrations; for Private we can integrate with your HSM/KMS via standard keywrap, and no token storage by default unless you enable caching. There's some nuance around KV cache and prefix caching for latency-sensitive workloads.
[01:48] Samir Patel: When you say KV cache, is that like a sticky session cache on GPU? Curious how that affects multi-tenant setups.
[01:56] Diego Alvarez: Right — it's the per-request attention cache, so for a given session we keep the KV state in memory to avoid recomputing. For multi-tenant you can isolate by container/instance or run shared kernels with policy isolation; Dedicated pools make isolation simpler.
[02:12] Tom Becker: Are there strong hardware prescriptions? We run a mix — some A100-class, some cheaper 80GB Ampere instances and a few experimental H100s.
[02:20] Maya Chen: We publish recommended profiles; Redwood's runtime is architecture-aware and will select kernels by device. For channel partners we often recommend certifying 1-2 SKU profiles for predictable perf.
[02:33] Lena Novak: One of our telco customers is very strict on SOC 2 and audit trails, and they ask for full request logs retained for 90 days but access-restricted. How does Redwood handle logs and PII?
[02:45] Diego Alvarez: We can enable audit log retention and RBAC, and for Private deployments logs can remain in your VPC and integrated with your SIEM. Some of our customers also use token redaction and field-level obfuscation for PII. Note: our hosted logs are multi-tenant and we do provide SOC 2 reports but if you need on-prem audit logs that's supported in Private.
[03:05] Samir Patel: Ok good. Pricing question — for a bundle where PV re-sells to end customers, what's typical margin split? Also pilot pricing?
[03:15] Maya Chen: We have partner-friendly referral and reseller programs; exact split depends on commit level. For pilots we typically offer discounted Dedicated capacity or a small hosted credit; we can follow up with standard program terms.
[03:28] Tom Becker: We want a clear path to POC — ideally a two-week latency/cost benchmark with one telco customer. What minimal infra would you need?
[03:38] Diego Alvarez: For that we'd want: a representative model and prompt set, target QPS, target sequence lengths, and infra access (either test VPC peering or sample machines). If you're doing on-prem we can run the benchmark in your environment or provide a turnkey Dedicated pool.
[03:55] Lena Novak: We can share a topology diagram, but a question on networking — many of our sites use NAT and private ranges, can Redwood Private handle peering with no public egress?
[04:05] Diego Alvarez: Yes; Private supports VPC peering and direct connect styles, no mandatory public egress. You can run the control plane separately or via a private control plane options if needed. There are some firewall rules for health checking and telemetry but we can document those.
[04:20] Samir Patel: Awesome. A bit of pushback: our ops team is wary of managing long-lived kernels and serialization of models; they'd rather we consume a hosted like API. How heavy is the ops lift for Private?
[04:31] Maya Chen: Fair. Private is heavier operationally but Redwood provides an on-prem package with install scripts, helm charts, and optional managed support. Also Dedicated is a middle ground — we run the infra and you get isolated pools with SLAs.
[04:45] Tom Becker: Curious about failover — suppose a Dedicated pool hits capacity, how do you route?
[04:50] Diego Alvarez: We have smart routing — we can failover to a compatible lower-cost model or spill to hosted. For partners we can configure routing policies and quotas per-customer to avoid surprise bills.
[05:05] Samir Patel: That could work. On compliance, we need a SOC two report and a small security questionnaire completed before pilots.
[05:12] Maya Chen: We'll share SOC 2 Type II and a red-team summary. I'll get that to you.
[05:18] Lena Novak: Thanks. Another nit: some of our customers require SAML/SSO integration and fine-grained RBAC into the inference console. Is that supported?
[05:27] Diego Alvarez: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported and RBAC can be mapped to groups. For private deployments you can integrate with your IdP directly.
[05:36] Tom Becker: What about model updates and version pinning? If a customer wants to pin a model for predictability during a pilot, can they lock to a version?
[05:44] Maya Chen: Absolutely. We support model version pinning and controlled rollouts (canary/A-B). That helps prevent regressions during pilots.
[05:52] Samir Patel: Ok let's talk timeline. If we want a two-week pilot in late August, what's the lead time to have a Dedicated pool or Private instance ready?
[06:01] Diego Alvarez: Dedicated pool can be provisioned in 2-3 weeks given capacity availability; Private on-prem depends on your infra readiness — if you have machines and network done it's about 1-2 weeks of install + config.
[06:11] Tom Becker: Are there specific metrics we should capture during the pilot to evaluate economics?
[06:16] Maya Chen: Yes — cost per 1k tokens, median and 99th perc latency for targeted prompts, GPU utilization, and cache hit rate. We can provide a template.
[06:26] Samir Patel: Good. We also want to know about quantization and model size tradeoffs — some of our clients want smaller footprint.
[06:33] Diego Alvarez: We have quantized runtime options and recommendations per model; quantization reduces memory but can affect quality — we can run an eval set to measure.
[06:41] Maya Chen: We'll include a quick quantization tradeoff table in the docs we share.
[06:46] Lena Novak: One operational question — how do you support upgrades? We have strict maintenance windows.
[06:51] Diego Alvarez: We support scheduled upgrades and can orchestrate canary+rollback; for Private we respect your maintenance windows and can perform offline upgrades.
[06:59] Samir Patel: Cool. Any red flags from your side about our infra?
[07:03] Diego Alvarez: Nothing immediate; just want to see the network diagram and whether you have private peering or a colocation hop. Also to confirm if you have HSM/KMS endpoints for customer keywrap.
[07:15] Tom Becker: We'll provide diagrams.
[07:18] Maya Chen: Quick note — we sometimes see partners want to bake their own auth in front of hosted API which can lead to added latency and rate-limit issues. Might be worth discussing an architecture where auth is delegated to your gateway but tokens are short-lived.
[07:33] Samir Patel: Makes sense. On margins, do you offer referral fees vs discounted resell?
[07:38] Maya Chen: Both. Referral is easier initially; reseller requires contract and commit. We'll share program options.
[07:45] Lena Novak: Any partner enablement — docs/training?
[07:48] Maya Chen: Yes, we have partner onboarding kits, technical enablement sessions, and a partner portal with docs and example Helm charts.
[07:57] Tom Becker: Ok — one last technical thing: our telco customer will need a 99.9% availability SLA and 95th/99th latency guarantees. Is that realistic?
[08:06] Diego Alvarez: 99.9% is achievable with Dedicated plus multi-az redundancy and autoscaling. For strict latency SLOs at 99th, you may need pinned instances, warmed KV cache, and careful routing; we can outline the architecture costs.
[08:23] Samir Patel: Great. I think this is heading to a good pilot.
[08:26] Maya Chen: Recap of next steps — we'll send a partner deck, SOC 2, private deployment docs, and a pilot checklist; Diego will draft an initial perf/cost matrix; Samir/Lena will share infra diagrams and confirm pilot customer and budget.
[08:41] Tom Becker: Sounds good. Proposed follow-up: technical scoping session Aug 4 with engineers.
[08:46] Maya Chen: We'll put that on the calendar — Aug 4 suggested.
[08:49] Samir Patel: Thanks all.
[08:51] Maya Chen: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with materials tomorrow.
[08:55] END
